title: She Danced in Bollywood Blockbusters. On Friday, She Performs at the World Cup.
excerpt: Nora Fatehi, the Moroccan-Canadian actress who became one of Indian cinema's biggest dance stars, takes the stage at Canada's FIFA World Cup opening ceremony in Toronto — a landmark moment for the diaspora.
body:
She made her name in Bollywood. On Friday night, she takes the stage at the biggest sporting event on the planet.

Nora Fatehi, the Moroccan-Canadian dancer and actress who became one of Indian cinema's most recognisable performers over the past decade, is among the headline acts at Canada's FIFA World Cup 2026 opening ceremony at BMO Field in Toronto. The ceremony, which begins at 1:30 PM ET on Friday, precedes Canada's Group B opener against Bosnia and Herzegovina.

It is a moment that bridges two worlds Fatehi has straddled throughout her career — and one that will resonate deeply with the millions of Indian and South Asian diaspora fans watching from living rooms across North America, the UK, and the Gulf.

From Casablanca to Mumbai to the World Cup Stage

Born in 1992 in Casablanca, Morocco, Fatehi moved to Canada as a teenager before relocating to Mumbai in her early twenties with a singular ambition: to break into Bollywood. The path was unconventional and anything but smooth. She appeared in a string of minor roles before her dance abilities caught the attention of choreographers and producers alike.

The breakthrough arrived in 2018 with "Dilbar Dilbar," a reimagined version of the 1999 Sushmita Sen classic that became the first Hindi song to cross 20 million views on YouTube within 24 hours of release. The music video has since surpassed two billion views. It was followed by a string of chart-topping dance numbers — "O Saki Saki," "Garmi," "Kusu Kusu" — that cemented Fatehi as the most in-demand dance performer in contemporary Bollywood.

Her journey from outsider to one of the Indian film industry's most bankable names mirrors the broader story of cross-cultural fluency that defines the diaspora experience. A Moroccan passport holder who built a career in India and now returns to perform for her adopted home country at the World Cup — it is a trajectory that few could have scripted.

A Lineup That Reflects Canada's Diversity

Fatehi joins a lineup that reads like a map of Canada's multicultural fabric. Michael Bublé, the Vancouver-born crooner, headlines the ceremony. He is joined by Alanis Morissette, Alessia Cara, and Jessie Reyez — each representing different eras and styles of Canadian pop music. Palestinian-Chilean singer Elyanna adds a Middle Eastern dimension, while French artist Vegedream will perform "Ramenez la coupe à la maison," the anthem that soundtracked France's 2018 World Cup victory.

Sanjoy, a Bangladeshi-American DJ and producer, rounds out the South Asian representation on the bill. For a country that is home to 1.8 million people of Indian origin — the largest South Asian diaspora in the Western hemisphere after the United States — the inclusion of Fatehi and Sanjoy on a global stage is not merely symbolic. It is a statement about who Canada sees itself as in 2026.

Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

The ceremony kicks off at 11 PM IST for viewers in India, available on Zee5 and UNITE8 Sports as part of FIFA's broadcast deal with Z that runs through 2034. For the estimated 745 million football fans in India — a number that has surged in recent years — seeing a performer so deeply associated with Indian popular culture at the centre of a World Cup celebration is a cultural landmark.

Toronto's BMO Field, ranked the third-best World Cup host venue by Sports Illustrated, seats roughly 30,000 fans. The surrounding Greater Toronto Area is home to one of the densest concentrations of Indian diaspora families anywhere in the world. Brampton alone has a South Asian population exceeding 250,000. Many of those fans will be in the stands on Friday evening, watching one of Bollywood's biggest names perform before a FIFA World Cup match — in their city.

For the desi diaspora, the moment lands differently than it does for anyone else in the stadium. It is the rare convergence of a global sporting spectacle and a cultural touchstone from the world they grew up in — or the world their parents left behind. Nora Fatehi does not play for Canada. But for a few minutes at BMO Field on Friday, she will represent something just as powerful.
